questions.q: Which vertebral disease pattern indicates a BETTER prognosis in Pott's paraplegia?
questions.exp: Vertebral disease: active / exudative / wet -> better prognosis; healed -> bad. (Book p150)

questions.q: In Pott's paraplegia, a BETTER prognosis is seen when compression is due to:
questions.exp: Compression d/t granulation tissue -> better prognosis; compression d/t bony deformity -> bad. (Book p150)

questions.q: Which combination is MOST likely to give a POOR prognosis in Pott's paraplegia?
opts: Young, slow onset, early onset, active wet disease
Older, rapid onset, late onset, healed disease
Older, slow onset, short history of cord involvement
questions.exp: Older age + rapid + late onset + long cord involvement + healed vertebral disease = bad prognosis. (Book p150)

questions.q: The 'middle path' regimen for Pott's paraplegia is:
opts: ATT for 18-24 months + rest + brace (Taylor's brace)
questions.exp: Middle path regimen: ATT for 18-24 months + rest + brace (Taylor's brace). (Book p150)

questions.q: The brace used in the middle-path regimen of Pott's paraplegia is:
questions.exp: Brace: Taylor's brace. (Book p150)

questions.q: If the patient improves on the middle-path regimen, management is to:
questions.exp: Improvement -> continue treatment. (Book p150)

questions.q: Surgical decompression in Pott's paraplegia is indicated when there is:
opts: No improvement / neurological manifestation, or worsening / bowel and bladder involvement
questions.exp: No improvement / neurological manifestation, or worsening / bowel and bladder involvement -> surgical decompression. (Book p150)

questions.q: The surgical decompression for Pott's paraplegia consists of:
opts: Left anterolateral decompression + autologous bone grafting + spine stabilisation
questions.exp: Surgical decompression: left anterolateral decompression + autologous bone grafting + spine stabilisation. (Book p150)

questions.q: During Pott's paraplegia decompression, all of the following parts are removed EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Parts removed: rib, transverse process, pedicle, vertebral body, affected disc. (Book p150)

questions.q: On MRI, a involved disc ('bad disc') in a lytic spine lesion suggests:
questions.exp: Disc involved (bad disc) -> TB spine (good prognosis). (Book p151)

questions.q: On MRI, a spared disc ('good disc') in a lytic spine lesion suggests:
questions.exp: Disc spared (good disc) -> metastasis (bad prognosis). (Book p151)

questions.q: The 'winking owl sign' on spinal X-ray indicates:
questions.exp: X-ray: metastasis -> winking owl sign. (Book p151)

questions.q: The winking owl sign is produced by:
questions.exp: Winking owl sign is d/t destruction of pedicle (absent pedicle). (Book p151)

questions.q: The site / first focus of appearance in TB hip is the:
questions.exp: Site / first focus of appearance: acetabulum and Babcock's triangle. (Book p151)

questions.q: Babcock's triangle is located in the:
questions.exp: Babcock's triangle: area in neck of femur. (Book p151)

questions.q: The organism grows easily in Babcock's triangle because it is:
questions.exp: Deficient in monocyte and macrophage -> organism grows easily. (Book p151)

questions.q: Local symptoms of TB hip include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Local symptoms: painful limb / antalgic gait, shortening, deformity. (Book p151)

questions.q: Stage I of TB hip is:
opts: Early arthritis / stage of apparent shortening
Late arthritis / stage of true shortening
questions.exp: Stage I: synovitis / stage of apparent lengthening. (Book p152)

questions.q: In stage I TB hip, the inflamed synovium causes:
opts: Increased synovial fluid secretion -> distension of capsule -> pain
questions.exp: Inflamed synovium -> increased synovial fluid secretion -> distension of capsule -> pain. (Book p152)

questions.q: The position of ease in early (stage I) TB hip is:
questions.exp: Position of ease: flexion, abduction, external rotation. (Book p152)

questions.q: Stage II of TB hip is:
opts: Early arthritis / stage of apparent shortening
questions.exp: Stage II: early arthritis / stage of apparent shortening. (Book p152)

questions.q: The apparent shortening in stage II TB hip is:
questions.exp: Stage II: apparent shortening <1 cm, with flexion, adduction, internal rotation. (Book p152)

questions.q: Stage III of TB hip is:
opts: Late arthritis / stage of true shortening
questions.exp: Stage III: late arthritis / stage of true shortening. (Book p152)

questions.q: True shortening in stage III TB hip is:
questions.exp: Stage III: true shortening >1 cm, with significant destruction of articular cartilage. (Book p152)

questions.q: In stage IV ('wandering acetabulum') TB hip, the destroyed femoral head appears as a small head against a large acetabulum - this is called:
questions.exp: Stage IV: destruction of head of femur (small head against large acetabulum) -> pestle and mortar deformity. (Book p152)

questions.q: Stage V of TB hip is:
opts: Fibrous ankylosis - painful, unstable hip with limited mobility
questions.exp: Stage V: fibrous ankylosis - painful, unstable hip with limited mobility. (Book p152)

questions.q: Phemister's triad in TB hip consists of all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Phemister triad: 1. juxta-articular osteopenia / osteoporosis, 2. peripheral osseous erosions, 3. narrowing of joint space. (Book p152)

questions.q: The earliest sign of TB hip on X-ray is:
questions.exp: Juxta-articular osteopenia / osteoporosis: earliest sign in X-ray (Phemister triad). (Book p152)

questions.q: Early treatment of TB hip is:
opts: ATT + rest + traction (prevent destruction of head)
questions.exp: Early: ATT + rest + traction (prevent destruction of head); no improvement -> surgical decompression. (Book p152)

questions.q: Late treatment of TB hip consists of:
opts: ATT + correction of deformity in fibrous ankylosis
questions.exp: Late: ATT + correction of deformity: in fibrous ankylosis. (Book p152)

questions.q: For correction of late TB hip with a MOBILE hip, the BEST option is:
questions.exp: Correction with mobile hip: arthroplasty - total hip replacement (best). (Book p152)

questions.q: Total hip replacement in late TB hip is usually performed after:
questions.exp: THA performed after 10-15 years d/t risk of recurrence. (Book p152)

questions.q: In Girdlestone excision arthroplasty:
opts: Fibrosed head of femur is removed and muscle interposed between neck and acetabulum; done when THA is contraindicated
questions.exp: Girdlestone: fibrosed head of femur removed, muscle interposed between neck and acetabulum; done when THA is contraindicated. (Book p152)

questions.q: Correction of late TB hip with a FIXED hip (fibrous ankylosis) is by:
questions.exp: Correction with fixed hip: arthrodesis. (Book p152)

questions.q: The attitude of the knee in TB knee is:
questions.exp: Attitude of knee: 5-30 degree flexion (position of ease d/t initial synovitis leading to effusion). (Book p153)

questions.q: The knee rests in 5-30 degree flexion in early TB knee because of:
questions.exp: Position of ease d/t initial synovitis leading to effusion. (Book p153)

questions.q: The triple deformity of late TB knee (PERF) consists of all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Triple deformity in late stage (PERF): 1. posterior subluxation of knee, 2. external rotation of tibia, 3. flexion of knee. (Book p153)

questions.q: The IOC for TB knee is:
questions.exp: MRI (IOC): synovitis seen. (Book p153)

questions.q: The gold standard for diagnosis of TB knee is:
questions.exp: Biopsy: gold standard. (Book p153)

questions.q: Early treatment of TB knee is:
opts: ATT + rest + traction (prevent destruction of head); no improvement -> surgical decompression
questions.exp: Early: ATT + rest + traction (prevent destruction of head); no improvement -> surgical decompression. (Book p153)

questions.q: Late treatment of TB knee includes correction of deformity by:
questions.exp: Late: ATT + correction of deformity -> arthroplasty (after 10-15 years) or arthrodesis. (Book p153)

questions.q: A non-healing sinus in chronic osteomyelitis is due to:
questions.exp: Non-healing sinus in chronic osteomyelitis: d/t presence of sequestrum. (Book p153)

questions.q: Periosteal reaction in tubercular osteomyelitis is:
questions.exp: Periosteal reaction not seen in tubercular osteomyelitis. (Book p153)

questions.q: The part of the vertebra LEAST involved in TB spine is the:
questions.exp: Part of vertebra least involved in TB spine: spinous process. (Book p153)

questions.q: Paraplegia in TB spine is commonest in the:
questions.exp: Paraplegia in TB spine commonest in upper thoracic region. (Book p153)

questions.q: Paraplegia is commonest in the upper thoracic region in TB spine because there the spinal cord is:
questions.exp: Upper thoracic region: spinal cord thicker -> easier to compress. (Book p153)

questions.q: Charcot's joint is seen in all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Charcot's joint seen in: syphilis, DM, syringomyelia. (Book p153)

units.title: TB of Bone: Introduction
units.guide: Koch's weak bacillus rides the blood from a primary focus - the lung - to settle in bone, where it rages far less than a pyogenes: less severe, paucibacillary, insidious. It picks the spine first (Pott's), then hip, then knee; within the spine dorso-lumbar beats dorsal beats lumbar, and children favour the cervical spine. The shoulder's dry 'caries sicca' and the fingers' air-filled 'spina ventosa' are the book's two named variants.

units.title: TB Spine: Four Types
units.guide: Pott's spine can strike four ways: paradiscally (the most common), centrally in the vertebral body, anteriorly - the wet exudative form of childhood - or posteriorly, the rarest of all. The paradiscal diagram lights up the para-vertebral bone and the disc between.

units.title: The Paradiscal Sandwich
units.guide: Paradiscal TB eats a three-bone sandwich: lower half of the upper vertebra, the disc, upper half of the lower vertebra - common somite, common sclerotome, common blood supply explain the triple hit. The lesion camps in front of the spinal cord, while the nerve slips out harmlessly through the intervertebral foramen.

units.title: Clinical Features
units.guide: The patient announces himself with low-grade fever, malaise, night pains and an evening temperature rise; the spine answers with back pain (earliest symptom) and paraspinal spasm (earliest sign). Spasm straightens the back into the military attitude with a cautious gait; collapse brings the cold abscess and a growing hump - one spinous process is a knuckle, two or three a gibbus, more than three an angular kyphosis.

units.title: Investigation & Complications
units.guide: The first X-ray whisper is narrowed disc space - disc destruction and dissection - later joined by a paravertebral abscess and vertebral lysis, but never by periosteal reaction, TB's tell-tale absence. MRI is the IOC, showing the disc and paradiscal disease in bone and cartilage; CT-guided biopsy remains the gold standard that names the organism. Left to itself, a neglected TB spine fuses into bony ankylosis - elsewhere in the body it fuses fibrously.

units.title: Pott's Paraplegia
units.guide: Pott's spine tightens its grip on the cord by three routes: granulation tissue pushing, inflammation swelling the cord, and a spinal artery thrombosis that can kill the cord within hours - rapid onset is the worst of the three. Early UMN signs (ankle clonus, exaggerated reflexes, extensor plantar) sound the alarm; bowel and bladder involvement late is the grave prognostic bell.

units.title: Prognostic Factors
units.guide: Prognosis runs on five dials: younger age, slow onset, early onset, short cord involvement (beyond 1 month is bad), and an active wet spine rather than a healed one. Compression by granulation tissue beats compression by bony deformity; the full recipe of older + rapid + late + longer + healed is the formula for despair.

units.title: Pott's: Middle Path & Surgery
units.guide: The middle path: ATT for 18-24 months, rest and Taylor's brace. Improvement means continue; no improvement, neurological signs, or bowel-bladder sinking means to theatre - left anterolateral decompression, autologous bone grafting and spine stabilisation, with rib, transverse process, pedicle, vertebral body and affected disc all removed from the path of the cord.

units.title: TB Spine vs Metastasis
units.guide: Two lytic spine lesions, one disc as judge: on MRI a bad disc (involved) declares TB spine with good prognosis, a good disc (spared) declares metastasis with bad prognosis. On the plain film metastasis winks - the winking owl sign of a destroyed, absent pedicle.

units.title: TB Hip: Focus & Features
units.guide: TB hip opens quietly in the acetabulum and in Babcock's triangle, the immunologically weak patch of the femoral neck where monocytes and macrophages are deficient and the bacillus grows easily. The local story is a painful limb with antalgic gait, shortening and deformity.

units.title: TB Hip: Five Stages
units.guide: Five stages from fluid to stone: I - synovitis, apparent lengthening, hip in flexion-abduction-external rotation as the distended capsule seeks ease; II - early arthritis, apparent shortening under 1 cm, hip swung to flexion-adduction-internal rotation; III - true shortening beyond 1 cm with cartilage loss; IV - small destroyed head against a large wandering acetabulum, the pestle and mortar; V - painful, unstable fibrous ankylosis.

units.title: TB Hip: Phemister & Treatment
units.guide: Phemister's triad writes the X-ray: juxta-articular osteopenia first, peripheral osseous erosions, then narrowing of the joint space. Early treatment is ATT + rest + traction to save the head, with surgical decompression if it fails; late, deformity is corrected - total hip replacement is best (but wait 10-15 years for recurrence risk), Girdlestone excision when THA is contraindicated, or arthrodesis for the fixed hip.

units.title: TB Knee
units.guide: The TB knee rests in 5-30 degrees of flexion - the position of ease for a joint that starts with synovitis and effusion. Late it locks into the PERF triple deformity: posterior subluxation of the knee, external rotation of the tibia, flexion of the knee. MRI (IOC) shows the synovitis, biopsy is gold standard; early ATT + rest + traction, late arthroplasty after 10-15 years or arthrodesis.

units.title: Cross-Chapter Notes
units.guide: Margin notes that cross chapters: a non-healing sinus in chronic osteomyelitis means a sequestrum; no periosteal reaction in tubercular osteomyelitis; the spinous process is the vertebral part TB spares; paraplegia strikes the upper thoracic spine where the cord is thickest and easiest to compress. And Charcot's painless joint belongs to syphilis, DM and syringomyelia.
